findings.before: What is laid beside the main dish. The past vowel a (lag) and -e: die.
findings.after: What is laid beside the main dish. -lage nouns take the a of liegen/lag (legen itself is regular: legte), and -e makes them die.
findings.why: lag is the past of liegen, not of legen (legen, legte, gelegt). As written it teaches a false past tense *lag for legen.

findings.before: His behaviour at dinner was impossible.
findings.after: His behaviour at dinner was appalling.
findings.why: unmöglich here means outrageous/unacceptable; 'impossible' is a calque and not natural English for behaviour.

findings.before: Who has changed my seat setting?
findings.after: Who has moved my seat?
findings.why: 'changed my seat setting' is unnatural English; 'moved/adjusted my seat' is what an English speaker says.

findings.before: adjust wrongly; block; disguise (die Stimme)
findings.after: move out of position, adjust (wrongly); block; disguise (die Stimme); sich verstellen: pretend, put on an act
findings.why: The reflexive sich verstellen (pretend) is a common, B2-relevant sense and is missing; 'adjust wrongly' is narrower than actual use (den Sitz verstellen is often neutral).

findings.before: Learn it as a word. be- makes the thing you order the direct object: Ich bestelle eine Pizza.
findings.after: Learn it as a word.
findings.why: The second sentence explains nothing: stellen already takes a direct object, so be- does not 'make' the object here. It is a pseudo-explanation.

findings.before: Der Bote stellt das Paket morgen zu.
findings.after: Der Paketbote stellt das Paket morgen zu.
findings.why: Bare 'der Bote' sounds dated/literary; in everyday German it is der Paketbote (or die Post stellt … zu).

findings.before: C1
findings.after: B2
findings.why: einen Kurs belegen, belegte Brötchen, der Platz ist belegt are everyday B1/B2 usage; C1 overstates it.

findings.before: fill (a roll); take (a course); prove (with evidence)
findings.after: take (a course); prove, back up (with evidence); put a topping on (belegtes Brötchen); occupy (a seat: belegt)
findings.why: Most common senses first; 'fill (a roll)' is the least useful as a lead sense, and 'occupy/taken' (belegt) is missing though the why mentions it.

findings.before: Aus Grundsatz leihe ich niemandem Geld.
findings.after: Er hat strenge Grundsätze und hält sich daran.
findings.why: 'Aus Grundsatz' exists but a native would say 'aus Prinzip' or 'grundsätzlich'; the example should show Grundsatz in its typical use (Grundsätze haben, ein wichtiger Grundsatz).

findings.before: On principle I don't lend anyone money.
findings.after: He has strict principles and sticks to them.
findings.why: Follows the replaced example.

findings.before: das Gesetz: a ge- noun, so das, not der like most bare-stem nouns.
findings.after: das Gesetz: many ge- nouns are das (das Gesetz, das Gebäude), but not all (der Geruch, der Gewinn, der Gedanke).
findings.why: 'a ge- noun, so das' overgeneralises; many common ge- nouns are masculine.

findings.after: Used without an object (we cross over) it takes sein: Wir sind mit der Fähre übergesetzt.
findings.why: The intransitive use (ist übergesetzt) is at least as common as the transitive; the learner should know the helper switches.

findings.before: C2
findings.after: B2
findings.why: gute Vorsätze (fürs neue Jahr) is common everyday German; C2 is far too high.

findings.before: ist angegangen
findings.after: hat/ist angegangen
findings.why: The example and lead senses take haben: 'Das hat dich nichts angegangen', 'Wir haben das Problem angegangen'. Only the light/fire sense ('Das Licht ist angegangen') takes sein. Showing only 'ist' teaches a wrong Perfekt for the main sense.

findings.after: Concern, tackle: hat angegangen (Wir haben das Problem angegangen). A light going on: ist angegangen.
findings.why: Spell out the haben/sein split by sense, as is done for ausziehen and umziehen.

findings.before: ist gezogen
findings.after: hat/ist gezogen
findings.why: 'Pull' (the first sense and the example 'Du musst die Tür ziehen') takes haben: 'Ich habe die Tür gezogen'. Only 'move (house)' takes sein ('Wir sind nach Berlin gezogen'). The family header itself says hat/ist.

findings.before: adv
findings.after: conj
findings.why: Duden and DWDS class beziehungsweise as a conjunction (Konjunktion). It links like oder and takes up no position in the clause: 'Ich komme morgen beziehungsweise übermorgen.' The id already says .conj.

findings.before: give up; post (a parcel); place (an ad)
findings.after: give up; post (a parcel); set (homework, a task); place (an ad)
findings.why: 'Hausaufgaben aufgeben' (set homework) is common and is the sense that die Aufgabe comes from. Without it, the link aufgeben → Aufgabe ('task') looks arbitrary.

findings.before: T
findings.after: M
findings.why: 'Task' cannot be read off 'give up'. It comes from aufgeben = set (a task), a sense the learner hasn't met on the card. That is one figurative step, so M, not T.

findings.before: to give, to state (details); to show off
findings.after: to state (details, on a form); to show off
findings.why: 'to give' on its own points to plain geben, which is in the same family. Drop it so the clue leads only to angeben.

findings.before: nach = behind: give way and fall in behind.
findings.after: nach = after: you give way after pushing back, and yield to pressure (a rope or floor also gibt nach).
findings.why: 'fall in behind' is a made-up picture, and it does not explain 'give in'. The physical sense (der Boden gibt nach = the floor gives way) is the clearer bridge.

findings.before: result in; sich ergeben: arise; surrender
findings.after: yield, show, come to (a result: Die Umfrage ergab …); sich ergeben: arise, follow (from); surrender
findings.why: Without sich, ergeben mostly means 'yield, show, come to' ('Die Untersuchung ergab, dass …'; 'Das ergibt 100 Euro'). 'Result in' is a loose fit.

findings.before: C1
findings.after: B2
findings.why: 'Daraus ergibt sich …' and 'Die Studie ergab …' are standard in B2 reading and Goethe B2 texts. C1 overstates it, given that das Ergebnis is B1.

findings.before: C1
findings.after: B2
findings.why: 'Können Sie mir herausgeben?' (give change) is everyday shop language, and 'ein Buch herausgeben' is common in B2 texts. C1 is too high.

findings.before: surroundings, the area around; environment
findings.after: surroundings, the area around; (computing) environment
findings.why: A bare 'environment' invites the classic learner error *Umgebung for the natural environment, which is die Umwelt. In everyday use Umgebung means surroundings or neighbourhood; 'environment' is right only in a technical sense (Entwicklungsumgebung).

findings.before: Die Ankunft des Zuges verspätet sich um zehn Minuten.
findings.after: Die Ankunft des Zuges verzögert sich um zehn Minuten.
findings.why: Trains are late ('Der Zug verspätet sich'); an arrival is delayed ('die Ankunft verzögert sich'). Station announcements say 'verzögert sich'. 'Die Ankunft verspätet sich' is a slight collocation clash.

findings.before: Der Dieb entkommt durch das Fenster.
findings.after: Der Dieb ist durch das Fenster entkommen.
findings.why: A one-off escape is reported in the Perfekt. The present reads like stage directions. The Perfekt also shows the learner the sein helper (ist entkommen).

findings.before: The thief escapes through the window.
findings.after: The thief escaped through the window.
findings.why: Matches the Perfekt example.

findings.before: Mit Englisch kommt man hier gut durch.
findings.after: Hier ist so viel Verkehr, wir kommen nicht durch.
findings.why: The clue gives 'get through (a crowd, an exam)', but the example shows the 'get by' sense. The example should match the sense the clue teaches; otherwise 'get by' competes with auskommen's clue in the same family.

findings.before: You can get by here with English.
findings.after: There is so much traffic here, we can't get through.
findings.why: Matches the new example.

findings.before: come later, follow
findings.after: come later, follow; comply with (einer Bitte, einer Pflicht nachkommen)
findings.why: The dative 'comply with' sense is very frequent in written and official German (B2 letters), and it is not derivable from 'come later'.

findings.before: Wir haben am Strand den Sonnenuntergang angeschaut.
findings.after: Wir haben uns am Strand den Sonnenuntergang angeschaut.
findings.why: In standard German, 'etwas anschauen' in the sense of watching or looking at takes the reflexive dative: 'sich etwas anschauen'. Without 'uns' it sounds regional or clipped.

findings.before: sich beziehen auf: refer to; das Bett beziehen: put sheets on
findings.after: sich beziehen auf: refer to; receive (Gehalt, Rente beziehen); das Bett beziehen: put sheets on
findings.why: 'Rente/Arbeitslosengeld/Gehalt beziehen' is a high-frequency sense in official German and in news. It is missing.

findings.before: I am writing about your advertisement.
findings.after: I am writing with reference to your advertisement.
findings.why: Keeps the 'refer' meaning visible in the translation while staying natural letter English.

findings.before: draw (curtains) closed
findings.after: draw (curtains) closed; sich etwas zuziehen: catch (an illness), sustain (an injury)
findings.why: 'Sich eine Erkältung/Verletzung zuziehen' is a common sense (B2) that cannot be derived from closing curtains.

findings.before: widersprÜchlich
findings.after: wIdersprüchlich
findings.why: Derived from the noun Widerspruch and keeps its stress on wi- (Duden: wi̲dersprüchlich), unlike the verb widersprechen.

findings.before: Stressed on the stem: widersprüchlich.
findings.after: Stressed like der Widerspruch, on wi-: WIdersprüchlich (the verb widersprEchen is stressed on sprech).
findings.why: The note teaches the wrong stress.

findings.before: dementsprEchend
findings.after: dEmentsprechend
findings.why: Duden marks main stress on dem- (de̲mentsprechend); this is also the usual spoken stress. Stress on sprech is a secondary/emphatic variant.

findings.before: Stressed like entsprechend, on sprech.
findings.after: Main stress on dem-: DEMentsprechend.
findings.why: The note teaches the wrong stress.

findings.before: gEgebenenfalls
findings.after: gegEbenenfalls
findings.why: Stress follows the participle gegEben: Duden gege̲benenfalls. The first ge- is unstressed.

findings.before: B2
findings.after: A2
findings.why: Clear misfit: 'Danke, ebenfalls!' is everyday A2 language and ebenfalls is very frequent (wordfreq 5.3).

findings.before: C2
findings.after: C1
findings.why: Common in news (soziales Gefälle, Lohngefälle); C1 is a better fit than C2.

findings.before: C2
findings.after: C1
findings.why: Frequent in written German (wordfreq 3.8); C1 fits better.

findings.before: C1
findings.after: B2
findings.why: Ausfall (Stromausfall, Zugausfall, Unterrichtsausfall) is everyday news and transport language; B2.

findings.before: C1
findings.after: B2
findings.why: 'Es fallen Kosten an' is standard B2 work/consumer German.

findings.before: to fall down (a person, and get hurt)
findings.after: to fall down, to fall over (a person, onto the ground)
findings.why: hinfallen does not imply getting hurt; the clue adds a false component.

findings.before: Im Herbst fallen die Blätter von den Bäumen ab.
findings.after: Im Herbst fallen die Blätter ab.
findings.why: With 'von den Bäumen' natives would just say 'fallen ... von den Bäumen'; the bare 'fallen die Blätter ab' is the typical use of abfallen.

findings.before: In autumn the leaves fall from the trees.
findings.after: In autumn the leaves fall off.
findings.why: Match the revised example.

findings.before: stand out, be noticed
findings.after: stand out, be noticed; (mir fällt auf) I notice
findings.why: The example uses the dative 'mir fällt auf' = I notice, the most frequent pattern; the meaning should show it.

findings.before: applause (formal; also der Applaus); approval
findings.after: applause; approval (also der Applaus)
findings.why: Beifall is neutral standard German, not formal; it is the normal word in news reports.

findings.before: Am Ende hat es lauten Beifall gegeben.
findings.after: Am Ende gab es lauten Beifall.
findings.why: Präteritum 'gab es' is the natural form in narration; Perfekt of 'es gibt' is clumsy here.

findings.before: Learn it as a word. The old picture: you fall in beside someone, you side with them and clap.
findings.after: Learn it as a word. The old picture: you 'fall in beside' someone, i.e. take their side and approve; the applause sense came later.
findings.why: 'and clap' is not part of the historical picture; beifallen meant to side with someone.

findings.before: Der Bus hält hier nicht an.
findings.after: Können Sie hier bitte kurz anhalten?
findings.why: For a scheduled bus stop natives say 'Der Bus hält hier nicht'; anhalten is typically 'bring/come to a stop' (a driver, a car). The current example also repeats the base-verb example.

findings.before: The bus does not stop here.
findings.after: Could you stop here for a moment, please?
findings.why: Match the revised example.

findings.before: The family sticks together closely.
findings.after: The family has a strong sense of togetherness.
findings.why: The translation paraphrases with the verb; keep the noun so the learner sees what Zusammenhalt maps to.

findings.before: The police check that the rules are kept.
findings.after: The police check that the rules are being followed.
findings.why: 'rules are kept' is not idiomatic English; 'followed/observed'.

findings.before: I have a meeting with my boss tomorrow.
findings.after: I have a talk with my boss tomorrow.
findings.why: 'meeting' is the clue/meaning of Besprechung in this same family; translating Gespräch as 'meeting' blurs the two.

findings.before: B2
findings.after: B1
findings.why: krankschreiben / sich krankschreiben lassen is B1 everyday work language, and the noun Krankschreibung is already B1.

findings.before: B2
findings.after: B1
findings.why: Copying homework is school-everyday language; B1.

findings.before: sich etwas ansehen: look at, watch
findings.after: look at (jemanden ansehen); sich etwas ansehen: have a look at, watch
findings.why: The plain transitive use (Sie sah mich an = she looked at me) is the most frequent sense and is missing; only the reflexive sich etwas ansehen is given.

findings.before: Sie sieht vom Buch auf.
findings.after: Sie sieht von ihrem Buch auf.
findings.why: A native says 'von ihrem Buch' (or 'von der Zeitung'); 'vom Buch' sounds clipped, and exEn already says 'her book'.

findings.after: The verb is fairly literary (everyday: aufblicken, hochsehen). Much more common is the noun das Aufsehen: stir, sensation (Aufsehen erregen).
findings.why: The learner will meet das Aufsehen (Aufsehen erregen, aufsehenerregend) far more often than the verb.

findings.before: realise, accept
findings.after: realise, accept (a mistake); inspect, view (files, records: Akten einsehen)
findings.why: The administrative sense (Unterlagen/Akten einsehen) is common in official German and links to die Einsicht 'access (to files)' already listed there.

findings.before: to plan, to provide for (a plan)
findings.after: to provide for, to plan (what a rule or plan includes)
findings.why: '(a plan)' reads as the object of 'provide for'; in German the plan/law is the subject (Der Plan sieht ... vor). The current clue is circular and slightly misleading.

findings.after: sich vorsehen (vor): be careful (of), look out (for); hence die Vorsicht.
findings.why: Die Vorsicht's note relies on sich vorsehen, which is not shown on the verb itself.

findings.before: C1
findings.after: B2
findings.why: Einsicht (zur Einsicht kommen, Einsicht in Akten) is standard B2 vocabulary; it is also on the B2 board.

findings.before: T
findings.after: M
findings.why: an + Sicht literally gives 'a view onto something'; 'opinion' is one figurative step, the same reasoning used for Aussicht (M).

findings.before: B2
findings.after: A2
findings.why: Learners meet (Auf) Wiedersehen at A1; das Wiedersehen as a noun is B1 at most.

findings.before: ersehen; besehen; hinsehen; wegsehen
findings.after: ersehen; besehen; hinsehen; wegsehen; die Durchsicht (inspection, check-through); die Nachsicht (leniency); durchsichtig (transparent); einsichtig (reasonable, understanding)
findings.why: The boards make these buildable (B1: nach + t = Nachsicht; B2: durch + t = Durchsicht, durch/ein + t + ig). All are common standard words (DWDS entries, wordfreq ~3) and must never be met with silence or treated as wrong.

findings.after: There is also an inseparable durchfAhren (hat durchfahren): travel through, cross (ein Land durchfahren).
findings.why: Like umfahren, durchfahren has a stressed-separable and an unstressed-inseparable reading; the sheet already teaches the pair for umfahren.

findings.before: Er überfährt eine rote Ampel.
findings.after: Beinahe hätte er eine Katze überfahren.
findings.why: The example illustrates only the second sense; the first and main sense 'run over' has no example. (The red-light sentence is correct but legal/news register.)

findings.before: Auf der Hinfahrt hat unser Zug Verspätung gehabt.
findings.after: Auf der Hinfahrt hatte unser Zug Verspätung.
findings.why: With haben natives almost always use the Präteritum (hatte); 'hat Verspätung gehabt' sounds clumsy.

findings.before: Die Fahrerin des Busses ist sehr freundlich.
findings.after: Die Busfahrerin ist sehr freundlich.
findings.why: 'Die Fahrerin des Busses' is stiff; natives use the compound. If the bare form must stay: 'Unsere Fahrerin ist sehr freundlich.'

findings.before: B2
findings.after: B1
findings.why: Fahrzeug is on the Goethe B1 word list and in every traffic/announcement text.

findings.before: zerfahren; entfahren; widerfahren; anfahren; auffahren; ausfahren
findings.after: zerfahren; entfahren; widerfahren; anfahren; auffahren; ausfahren; die Überfahrt (crossing); die Durchfahrt (passage, way through: Durchfahrt verboten); die Weiterfahrt (onward journey); die Vorbeifahrt (driving past); der Mitfahrer (passenger, fellow traveller); die Mitfahrt (ride, lift); der Ausfahrer (delivery driver)
findings.why: The B1/B2 boards (über/durch/weiter/vorbei/mit/aus + t/er) can build these; Überfahrt, Durchfahrt, Weiterfahrt and Mitfahrer are everyday words (wordfreq 3+).

findings.after: In southern Germany, Austria and Switzerland: ist gestanden.
findings.why: The learner will hear 'ist gestanden' constantly in the south; worth flagging as regional so it is not taken as an error.

findings.before: pass (an exam); bestehen aus: consist of
findings.after: pass (an exam); bestehen aus: consist of; bestehen auf: insist on; exist
findings.why: bestehen auf (insist on) and bestehen = exist (seit 1990 bestehen) are both high-frequency B1/B2 senses and are needed for der Bestand's 'why' (bestehen = exist).

findings.before: Ich bestehe die Prüfung.
findings.after: Ich habe die Prüfung bestanden!
findings.why: A bare present 'Ich bestehe die Prüfung' is unnatural out of context; natives say 'Ich habe ... bestanden' or 'Hoffentlich bestehe ich die Prüfung'. exEn then: 'I passed the exam!'

findings.before: Ich widerstehe der Schokolade.
findings.after: Ich kann der Schokolade einfach nicht widerstehen.
findings.why: The bare statement is stilted; widerstehen typically appears in 'nicht widerstehen können'. exEn: 'I just can't resist the chocolate.'

findings.before: B1
findings.after: B2
findings.why: Ruhestand is formal (everyday: Rente, in Rente gehen); B2 fits better. Not on a board, so minor.

findings.before: erstehen; anstehen; zustehen
findings.after: erstehen; anstehen; zustehen; der Aufstand (uprising); der Ausstand (strike); der Überstand (overhang, projection); umständlich (complicated, long-winded); beständig (constant, stable); die Beständigkeit (constancy); verständig (sensible); geständig (having confessed: der Täter ist geständig); widerständig (resistant, rebellious)
findings.why: The B1/B2 boards (auf/aus/über/um/be/ver/ge/wider + stem/ig/lich/keit) can build these; umständlich (wordfreq 3.5), beständig and Aufstand are very common words. Not listing them risks a correct real word getting no credit.

findings.before: decide (formally), resolve; pass (a law)
findings.after: decide, resolve; pass (a law, a budget)
findings.why: beschließen is the normal everyday verb for a firm decision (the sheet's own example: Wir haben beschlossen, nach Berlin umzuziehen). 'Formally' teaches a false register restriction and contradicts the example.

findings.before: to decide formally; to pass (a law)
findings.after: to decide (to do something); to pass (a law)
findings.why: Follows from the en fix; it stays distinct from sich entschließen ('make up your mind (sich)') and der Beschluss ('the resolution').

findings.before: B2
findings.after: B1
findings.why: beschließen is Goethe B1 vocabulary; it is already used on the B1 board.

findings.before: adv
findings.after: prep (+ Gen.), adv
findings.why: In the example (80 Euro einschließlich Frühstück) and in almost all use, einschließlich is a preposition (einschließlich der Mehrwertsteuer, + Genitiv; bare noun without article). Labelling it adv misinforms the learner about how it governs case.

findings.before: C1
findings.after: B2
findings.why: ausschließlich is frequent (wordfreq ~4) in signs and notices; B2 at most.

findings.before: C1
findings.after: B2
findings.why: Beschluss (einen Beschluss fassen) is standard B2 news vocabulary, and it is on the B2 board.

findings.before: A2
findings.after: A1
findings.why: schließen (Tür/Fenster schließen) is A1 on the Goethe list.

findings.before: Board B1: abschließen.verb, der_Abschluss, anschließen.verb, der_Anschluss, ausschließen.verb, beschließen.verb, aufschließen.verb, sich_entschließen.verb, der_Entschluss, die_Schließung
findings.after: Board B1: abschließen.verb, der_Abschluss, anschließen.verb, der_Anschluss, ausschließen.verb, beschließen.verb, aufschließen.verb, einschließen.verb, der_Schluss, geschlossen.adj (or keep sich_entschließen/der_Entschluss but drop die_Schließung)
findings.why: As levelled, the B1 board carries four B2 forms (beschließen, sich entschließen, Entschluss, Schließung) plus B2 ausschließen. Schließung especially is formal B2 and fits the B2 board, where it already is.

findings.after: der Aufschluss (information, insight: Aufschluss geben); der Einschluss (inclusion; enclosure); die Erschließung (development of land, a market); die Entschließung (formal resolution); die Einschließung; die Ausschließung; die Abschließung; die Verschließung
findings.why: The RARE list is empty although the boards can build several real, common words: auf/ein + stem (Aufschluss wordfreq 3.5, Einschluss), er/ent + ung (Erschließung wordfreq 3.7, Entschließung). These must never go unrecognised.

findings.before: on sale; bribable (a person)
findings.after: can be bought; bribable (a person)
findings.why: 'on sale' means discounted in English and also fits verkäuflich, which is on the same B2 board (clue 'saleable'), so the clue does not lead to one word.

findings.before: for sale, on sale; bribable, corrupt (a person)
findings.after: for sale, available to buy; bribable, corrupt (a person)
findings.why: 'on sale' in English usually means reduced in price, which käuflich does not mean.

findings.before: zuverlÄssig
findings.after: zUverlässig
findings.why: Duden marks the main stress on zu-: ZU-verlässig. The stress on -läss- is a possible variant but should not be the one taught.

findings.before: die ZuverlÄssigkeit
findings.after: die ZUverlässigkeit
findings.why: Same stress as zuverlässig: ZU-verlässigkeit (Duden).

findings.before: das Gesuch: a ge- noun, so das, not der.
findings.after: das Gesuch: neuter, unlike der Besuch and der Versuch. Learn the article with the word.
findings.why: There is no rule that ge- nouns are neuter: der Geruch, der Geschmack, der Gesang, der Gebrauch, der Genuss and der Gewinn are all masculine ge- + stem nouns. The note teaches a false rule.

findings.before: Im Winter lasse ich den Motor kurz an.
findings.after: Lass das Licht im Flur bitte an.
findings.why: 'den Motor kurz anlassen' is odd. 'Start the engine' is usually 'den Motor starten', and 'run it briefly' is 'kurz laufen lassen'. The leave-on sense is the common everyday use.

findings.before: In winter I start the engine for a moment.
findings.after: Please leave the light on in the hall.
findings.why: Goes with the new example.

findings.before: verb |  (split field empty)
findings.after: verb | SPLITS
findings.why: blaumachen is separable (Ich mache blau, hat blaugemacht, blauzumachen). The split field should say so, not only the note.

findings.before: Learn it as a word: what a doctor finds, from an older sense of befinden (to judge).
findings.after: Learn it as a word: what a doctor finds after an examination; befinden also means to judge, decide (formal: etwas für gut befinden).
findings.why: The sense 'judge, decide' is not old. It is still current formal German (für richtig befinden, über etwas befinden).

findings.before: I find my way around the new city well.
findings.after: I'm finding my way around the new city easily.
findings.why: 'find my way around ... well' is stiff English.

findings.before: on Board B1
findings.after: B2 board only
findings.why: Severance pay is a B2/C1 work-law term (level B2 here). It sits awkwardly on a B1 board next to Erfindung and stattfinden.

findings.before: Der Laden hat alle Winterjacken ausverkauft.
findings.after: Wegen der Schließung verkauft der Laden alles aus.
findings.why: The active perfect with a shop as subject is uncommon. Natives say 'Die Winterjacken sind ausverkauft'. The active verb is mostly used for clearance sales (alles ausverkaufen).

findings.before: The shop has sold out of all its winter jackets.
findings.after: Because it's closing, the shop is selling everything off.
findings.why: Goes with the new example.

findings.before: People say that he is very rich.
findings.after: He is said to be very rich.
findings.why: nachsagen is about reputation. 'He is said to be' keeps that sense better than plain 'people say'.

findings.before: the visitor (of a museum, a website)
findings.after: the visitor (to a museum, a website)
findings.why: In English it is 'visitor to', not 'visitor of'.

findings.before: These costs are no longer acceptable for us.
findings.after: We can no longer afford to bear these costs.
findings.why: tragbar for costs means bearable or sustainable. 'acceptable for us' is unidiomatic and misses the sense.

findings.before: Die Bank sucht Kunden, die pünktliche Zahler sind.
findings.after: Säumige Zahler bekommen eine Mahnung.
findings.why: The original is stilted. Zahler occurs mostly in set phrases: säumiger/pünktlicher Zahler.

findings.before: The bank is looking for customers who pay on time.
findings.after: People who pay late get a reminder.
findings.why: Goes with the new example.

findings.after: Not to be confused with der Zähler (meter, counter; numerator).
findings.why: Zahler and Zähler are a common learner mix-up.

findings.before: Wir zahlen den Kredit in zehn Jahren ab.
findings.after: Wir zahlen den Kredit über zehn Jahre ab.
findings.why: 'in zehn Jahren' first suggests 'ten years from now'. 'über zehn Jahre' (or 'innerhalb von zehn Jahren') matches 'over ten years'.

findings.before: After the statement came a big additional bill.
findings.after: The annual statement brought a large extra payment to make.
findings.why: The English uses German word order and is unnatural.

findings.before: I'm just quickly buying bread and milk.
findings.after: I'll just quickly get some bread and milk.
findings.why: 'noch schnell' means 'quickly before something else'. 'I'm just quickly buying' is awkward English.

findings.before: Meine Mutter arbeitet in einer Bank.
findings.after: Meine Mutter arbeitet bei einer Bank.
findings.why: For an employer, 'bei einer Bank arbeiten' is the idiomatic choice; 'in einer Bank' stresses the building.

findings.before: B1
findings.after: A2
findings.why: Inconsistent with die Arbeiterin (A2); Arbeiter is a basic A2 word.

findings.before: Sie arbeitet an dem neuen Projekt mit.
findings.after: Sie arbeitet am neuen Projekt mit.
findings.why: 'am' is the natural contraction here; 'an dem' sounds stressed/demonstrative.

findings.before: She is working on the new project too.
findings.after: She is helping out on (collaborating on) the new project.
findings.why: 'too' adds a meaning that is not in the German; mitarbeiten = take part in / contribute to the work.

findings.before: A1
findings.after: A2
findings.why: Mitarbeiter is not an A1 word; A2 (as die Mitarbeiterin) is fairer.

findings.before: editing; processing
findings.after: editing; handling (of a case, an application)
findings.why: 'processing' overlaps with die Verarbeitung (clue: 'the processing (of data, of food)'); keeping Bearbeitung as 'handling' separates the two for the learner.

findings.before: sich einarbeiten: get to know (a new job, a topic); work in (an ingredient)
findings.after: sich einarbeiten: settle in (to a new job), get to grips with (a topic); einarbeiten: train (new staff); work in (an ingredient)
findings.why: 'get to know' is weak and the non-reflexive senses are mixed under the reflexive label; jemanden einarbeiten (train someone in) is the common transitive sense and explains die Einarbeitung.

findings.before: Thank you for the good cooperation!
findings.after: Thank you for working with us so well!
findings.why: 'the good cooperation' is a literal calque; natural English rephrases (or: 'Many thanks for the great collaboration!').

findings.before: zerarbeiten; umarbeiten; nacharbeiten; vorarbeiten; zuarbeiten; herausarbeiten
findings.after: add: die Erarbeitung, die Abarbeitung, die Durcharbeitung (real -ung nouns buildable from the B2 tiles er/ab/durch + ung)
findings.why: Erarbeitung (154k DWDS hits) and Abarbeitung (18k) are real and can be built on the B2 board; they must never be called wrong.

findings.before: to get you further (that gets us nowhere)
findings.after: to help (someone) get further, to get somewhere
findings.why: The bracket gives the opposite sense and the English is awkward; a plain clue is clearer.

findings.after: add: angebracht (adj: appropriate), die Erbringung, die Anbringung, die Einbringung
findings.why: The B2 board has endings ung and pp; angebracht (very common adjective, 'appropriate'), Erbringung, Anbringung and Einbringung are real words buildable from the tiles. The RARE list is empty.

findings.before: Will you bring me a glass of water?
findings.after: Could you bring me a glass of water, please?
findings.why: 'bitte' is dropped; a polite request reads more naturally with could/please.

findings.before: What nationality is in your passport?
findings.after: What nationality does your passport say?
findings.why: More natural English.

findings.before: misshören; erhören; hinhören
findings.after: add: der Mithörer
findings.why: mit + hören + er is buildable on the B2 board; der Mithörer (eavesdropper, person listening in) is in DWDS.

findings.before: Im Lauf der Zeit hat sich viel verändert.
findings.after: Sie hat den Lauf über zehn Kilometer gewonnen.
findings.why: The clue asks for 'a run (a race)', but the example uses the 'course (of time)' sense in a fixed phrase (more usual: im Laufe der Zeit). Match example to clue, or change the clue to the course sense.

findings.before: hErumlaufen
findings.after: herUmlaufen
findings.why: herum is stressed on the second syllable (herúm): herúmlaufen, as heráus, hervór, vorbéi elsewhere in this sheet.

findings.after: Also inseparable: es überläuft mich kalt (a shiver runs over me); adjective überlaufen (not separable) = overcrowded (ein überlaufener Strand).
findings.why: The learner will meet the adjective überlaufen (stress on -lau-) often; worth marking it apart from the separable verb.

findings.before: zerlaufen; erlaufen; belaufen; widerlaufen
findings.after: add: vorlaufen, der Vorlauf, der Auslauf, der Einlauf, der Überlauf, der Ausläufer
findings.why: All are DWDS entries and buildable from the B1/B2 tiles (vor/aus/ein/über + stem/er); Vorlauf, Auslauf and Ausläufer are frequent.

findings.before: direct, aim (at); sich richten nach: go by, depend on
findings.after: direct, aim (at); sich richten an: be addressed to; sich richten nach: go by, depend on
findings.why: The example uses 'sich richten an' (be aimed at / addressed to), which is not in the meaning line.

findings.before: be- + richten (set right): you set someone right about what happened.
findings.after: be- + richten (put in order): you put someone in the picture about what happened.
findings.why: 'set someone right' in English means correct them, which is misleading for berichten (simply report/inform).

findings.before: zurichten; abrichten; vorrichten
findings.after: add: die Verrichtung, die Entrichtung, die Aufrichtung, die Herrichtung
findings.why: All are DWDS entries and buildable on the B2 board (ver/ent/auf/her + ung).

findings.before: to call out (a name); to open (a website)
findings.after: to call (the next patient, a name in a waiting room); to open (a website)
findings.why: 'call out' is also the meaning of ausrufen (en: 'call out, exclaim'), which is on the same B2 board; the clue must point only to aufrufen.

findings.before: B2
findings.after: B1
findings.why: der Anrufer is a simple, frequent word; B2 is too high.

findings.before: errufen; verrufen
findings.after: add: der Ausruf, der Abruf, die Ausrufung, die Anrufung, widerruflich
findings.why: All real (DWDS entries) and buildable from the B2 tiles (aus/ab/an/wider + stem/ung/lich); Abruf and Ausruf are common.

findings.before: C2
findings.after: C1
findings.why: Common in news reporting; C1 like the verb unterschlagen.

findings.before: abschlagen; beschlagen; verschlagen; entschlagen; überschlagen
findings.after: add: der Nachschlag, der Aufschlag, der Einschlag
findings.why: Nachschlag (second helping) is buildable on the A2/B1 boards (nach + stem), Aufschlag and Einschlag on the B2 board; all common real nouns.

findings.before: Die Teilung der Stadt dauerte fast dreißig Jahre.
findings.after: Die Teilung Deutschlands dauerte über vierzig Jahre.
findings.why: Read as Berlin, the division lasted about 41-45 years (1945/49-1990); 'fast dreißig Jahre' fits the Wall, not the division. Use a factually safe sentence (exEn: 'The division of Germany lasted over forty years.').

findings.before: The teacher divides the class into groups.
findings.after: The teacher does the dividing into groups.
findings.why: The translation drops the noun subject; a closer rendering keeps the learner's mapping.

findings.before: zerteilen; beteilen; beteiligen
findings.after: add: die Erteilung, die Zuteilung, die Unterteilung, die Austeilung, verteilbar
findings.why: All DWDS entries, buildable on the B2 board (er/zu/unter/aus/ver + ung/bar); Erteilung, Zuteilung and Unterteilung are frequent.

findings.before: Sie hat den alten Rekord um zwei Sekunden überboten.
findings.after: Sie hat den alten Rekord um zehn Zentimeter überboten.
findings.why: A time record is beaten by a LOWER time, which is unterbieten (and the family's own unterbieten entry teaches 'beat (a time)'). 'Rekord um zwei Sekunden überboten' contradicts that and confuses the über/unter contrast the board is built on; use a height/distance record.

findings.before: Learn it as a word: ver- turns offering into its opposite, forbidding.
findings.after: Like English for-bid: ver- (old for-) + bieten (bid, order) = forbid.
findings.why: The 'opposite of offering' story is invented; ver-bieten is the exact cognate of English for-bid, which is a far better memory hook. Grade could then be M rather than O.

findings.before: A bare stem with a vowel change, but das: an exception to learn.
findings.after: das, like all the -bot nouns (das Gebot, das Verbot, das Aufgebot): they come from das Gebot.
findings.why: Angebot/Verbot/Gebot/Aufgebot are regularly neuter (Ge- formation); presenting it as a one-off exception hides a usable pattern.

findings.before: In vielen Ländern gibt es ein Verbot für Plastiktüten.
findings.after: In vielen Ländern gibt es ein Verbot von Plastiktüten.
findings.why: 'Verbot von' (or the compound Plastiktütenverbot) is the more standard construction; 'Verbot für' tends to mean a ban that applies to a group of people (Verbot für Lkw).

findings.before: on Board B1
findings.after: B2 board only
findings.why: Darbietung is a formal B2/C1 word (stage/TV language); it is the least expected word on the B1 board. überbieten/unterbieten (B2) also sit high for B1.

findings.before: B2
findings.after: C1
findings.why: Formal register; typical learner lists put it at C1, and its own verb darbieten is marked C2.

findings.before: ist eingebrochen
findings.after: ist/hat eingebrochen
findings.why: Burglary sense: 'Diebe sind eingebrochen' is standard, but 'bei uns hat jemand eingebrochen' also occurs (Duden: ist/hat), and transitive 'eine Tür einbrechen' (smash in) takes hat.

findings.before: vomit, be sick (formal, medical)
findings.after: vomit, be sick (formal, medical; also sich erbrechen)
findings.why: Reflexive 'sich erbrechen' is at least as common as intransitive 'erbrechen' outside clinical notes; the learner should see both.

findings.before: C2 (RARE)
findings.after: C1
findings.why: gebrechlich is a common, unmarked word ('alt und gebrechlich', ~28k corpus hits); not C2/rare.

findings.before: Ich habe bei mehreren Firmen ein Angebot angefragt.
findings.after: Ich habe bei mehreren Firmen angefragt, ob sie noch Termine frei haben.
findings.why: Transitive 'ein Angebot anfragen' is business jargon (standard: ein Angebot anfordern / einholen); the core pattern to learn is 'bei jemandem anfragen, ob ...'. exEn: 'I asked several companies whether they still have appointments free.'

findings.before: Die niedrigen Preise verleiten viele Leute zum Kaufen.
findings.after: Die niedrigen Preise verleiten viele Leute zu Spontankäufen.
findings.why: 'zum Kaufen' is clumsy; 'jemanden zu etwas verleiten' normally takes a noun of the (unwise) act: zum Kauf, zu Spontankäufen. exEn: 'The low prices tempt many people into impulse buys.'

findings.before: An experienced colleague trains the new staff.
findings.after: An experienced colleague guides the new staff.
findings.why: 'trains' is closer to einarbeiten/ausbilden; anleiten = guide, instruct, matching the en and clue.

findings.before: notice, information; official decision (from an office)
findings.after: Bescheid sagen = let someone know; Bescheid wissen = know (about it); (official) notice, decision
findings.why: The everyday B1 use is in the fixed phrases Bescheid sagen/geben/wissen (which the example uses); 'notice, information' alone does not teach them.

findings.before: the official notice (from an office)
findings.after: the word in 'let me know' (... sagen); an official notice
findings.why: Clue sense (official decision) does not match the example sense (Sag mir Bescheid); the learner should meet the common one in the clue.

findings.before: I find it hard to keep work and free time apart.
findings.after: I find it hard to draw a line between work and free time.
findings.why: Closer to 'die Unterscheidung fällt mir schwer' (making the distinction), less of a paraphrase.

findings.before: the entry fee, admission
findings.after: the entry fee (at a museum, a concert)
findings.why: On the A2 board der_Zutritt has en 'access, admission'; 'admission' in this clue also fits Zutritt. Drop it to keep the two apart.

findings.after: Also an adjective: betreten (embarrassed, sheepish): betretenes Schweigen.
findings.why: The adjective homograph is common (betretenes Schweigen) and otherwise confusing when met.

findings.before: on Board A2
findings.after: B1/B2 boards only
findings.why: Four of six A2-board words are B1 (Tritt, Zutritt, Vertreter, betreten); Tritt is the least useful for an A2 learner.

findings.before: The text refers to a study.
findings.after: The text contains a reference to a study.
findings.why: Translate the noun as a noun so the learner sees Verweis = reference.

findings.before: Bewerber müssen drei Jahre Berufserfahrung vorweisen.
findings.after: Bewerber müssen drei Jahre Berufserfahrung vorweisen können.
findings.why: The set phrase in job ads is 'Berufserfahrung vorweisen können'; without können it sounds clipped.

findings.before: the proof (a document, a certificate)
findings.after: the certificate, the written proof (of income)
findings.why: On the B1 board der_Beweis's clue also starts 'the proof'; lead with 'certificate/written proof' so the two separate at a glance.
